opus-5.5.text:
I think Physical Intelligence is one of the more interesting experiments happening right now, precisely because they've chosen to behave like a research lab rather than a product company, at least for this stage.

What I appreciate is that they're quite open. They publish, they release models like π0 and the follow-ups, and they're honest about what works and what doesn't. In robotics that matters a lot, because the field has historically been fragmented: every lab has its own hardware, its own data, its own little benchmark. A group that's willing to put out a reasonably general recipe, a vision-language backbone plus an action head trained on lots of cross-embodiment data, and let others build on it, is doing something valuable for the whole community.

That said, I have some reservations about the VLA paradigm itself, and those apply to Pi as much as anyone. The basic bet is: take a pretrained vision-language model, attach actions, scale up robot data, and generalization will emerge the way it did for language. I'm not fully convinced. Language models work because text is already a compressed, symbolic representation of the world, and there's an internet's worth of it. Robot action data is tiny by comparison, expensive to collect, and tied to specific bodies. And the "vision" part of most VLAs is still fairly shallow. It's good at recognizing and naming things, but not necessarily at understanding space, physics, or how the world changes over time. That's the part I care about most from my own research perspective: I think visual representation and world modeling are still underdeveloped, and you can't just borrow them from a language model.

So my view is somewhat mixed. As a team and as a research culture, I think they're excellent, with very strong people and a willingness to tackle the hard, long-horizon problem instead of chasing a quick demo. But whether the current VLA recipe is the final answer, I'd be surprised. I suspect the field will need much better spatial and visual intelligence underneath, and maybe some form of learned world model, before we see the kind of robust generalization people are hoping for. The good news is that a research-oriented company is exactly the kind of place that can pivot when the evidence says so. That flexibility may end up being their biggest advantage.

fable-5.1.text:
Pi is interesting to me precisely because they chose not to be a product company first. Sergey Levine, Chelsea Finn, Karol Hausman, these are people who spent a decade in academia on robot learning, and they basically decided the bottleneck was no longer ideas, it was scale and data and infrastructure, and you can't get that inside a university lab anymore. So they built something that looks a lot like what OpenAI was in 2017 or 2018: a lab with a thesis, and the thesis is that general-purpose robot foundation models are possible and you should go straight at them.

I respect that bet, but I also want to be careful about it. In vision and language, we got the foundation model recipe because the internet handed us a data distribution that was already there. Robotics doesn't have that. Pi's answer has been to collect a lot of teleoperation data across many embodiments and then lean on a pretrained VLM as the backbone, and their pi-zero and the follow-up work with flow matching for action heads, that's genuinely nice engineering. The demos, the laundry folding and the kitchen cleanup, are not fake. They're real policies doing long-horizon things.

But if you ask me as a researcher, the open question is whether the vision-language part is actually doing the heavy lifting or whether it's mostly a good initialization and the real intelligence is coming from the action data. My own bias is that visual representation is still the weak link. These models can name objects and read instructions, but their spatial understanding, their sense of physics, of what's going to happen if you push this, is still shallow. I don't think you fix that only by collecting more trajectories. You need a visual backbone that actually understands the world, and that's a problem that cuts across robotics, not one Pi alone can solve.

The other thing I'd say is that Pi has been unusually open for a company of its kind. They publish papers, they released weights, and that matters, because the field needs shared baselines. A lot of what I'd call research credibility comes from that, not from the funding round. Whether that openness survives commercial pressure, I don't know. But right now, if you want a concrete object to argue with about what a VLA should be, Pi is one of the few places producing one.

astra-6.text:
I’d assess Pi along two dimensions: the research itself and whether that research translates into a system that works reliably. Those are related, but they’re not the same thing.

For a research-oriented VLA company, the interesting question is whether you’re building a model that can generalize across tasks and environments, rather than solving each new task through a lot of custom engineering. If more data and training consistently give you broader capabilities, that’s a very promising direction.

But robotics makes that difficult to judge. A compelling demonstration doesn’t tell you the success rate, how much intervention was needed, or what happens when the environment changes. I’d want to understand those things before making a strong assessment of Pi specifically.

The other question is the data loop. Can deploying the system generate useful experience that improves the next model? To me, the strongest research company would connect those pieces: research produces better robots, and operating those robots makes the research better.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d separate two questions: how strong is the research, and how well does it translate into a robotics business? For a research-oriented VLA company, the key question is whether its work produces capabilities that generalize beyond a particular robot, task, or carefully prepared setting.

A compelling demo is a starting point. What I’d want to understand is how much task-specific data and engineering went into it, what happens when the environment changes, and how reliably the system recovers from mistakes. Those details tell you much more about the underlying model.

So I’d assess Pi through that lens: is each research advance making it easier to learn the next task and deploy in the next environment? If that loop keeps improving, that’s a strong foundation. But I’d be cautious about making a firm judgment about the company without seeing that evidence.
